title: Tiwahe Tewichaglapi: Theater Testing of the Family Acceptance Project With Indigenous 2SLGBTQ+ Youth and Their Caregivers.
abstract: Research documents high rates of mental and behavioral health problems among Indigenous Two Spirit and LGBTQ+ (2SLGBTQ+) youth as a result of historic and ongoing colonialism, yet little is known about how to prevent these outcomes and promote wellness. Although family acceptance is a powerful protective factor, there is a lack of available interventions to support Indigenous 2SLGBTQ+ youth and their families. This study conducted community theater testing to engage Lakota 2SLGBTQ+ youth, their caregivers, and professionals who work with 2SLGBTQ+ youth to provide guidance to prepare to implement the Family Acceptance Project's (FAP) culture-based family support model with 2SLGBTQ+ youth and their caregivers. The program team conducted theater testing with 50 participants, including Lakota 2SLGBTQ+ youth (n = 25), caregivers of Lakota 2SLGBTQ+ youth (n = 15), and community members (n = 10). Participants viewed components of FAP's family support model, completed open- and closed-ended surveys, and participated in discussion to provide feedback on the content, cultural relevance, perceived impact, and interest in FAP's family support program. Participants expressed strong support for the FAP model and provided ideas on integrating Lakota cultural values, history, traditions, and community strengths into the program. Theater testing demonstrated that FAP's family support model is highly acceptable to Lakota 2SLGBTQ+ youth, their caregivers, and community members and provided important insights on integrating Lakota values and lived experiences-a core aspect of FAP's culture-based model. Findings underscore the importance of culturally grounded family interventions to reduce mental health disparities and promote well-being among Indigenous 2SLGBTQ+ youth.
